ACACIA: A thorny tree or shrub of warm regions; Australia's golden wattle is an acacia and its national flower.
ACORN: The nut of the oak tree, held in a little cup; it can take an oak 20 years to produce them.
AGAVE: A spiky succulent of Mexico; the blue agave is used to make tequila.
ALDER: A tree of riversides (genus Alnus) whose wood doesn't rot underwater; Venice is partly built on alder piles.
ALFALFA: A legume (Medicago sativa) grown to feed livestock; its name comes from Arabic, by way of Spanish.
ALGAE: Simple water plants, from pond scum to seaweed, that produce much of the world's oxygen.
ALMOND: A tree (Prunus dulcis) related to the peach, grown for its nut; most come from California.
ALOE: A succulent (Aloe vera among some 500 species) whose leaf gel soothes burns; native to Africa and Arabia.
AMARANTH: A plant with edible seeds and leaves, sacred to the Aztecs; its name is Greek for 'never fading'.
ANEMONE: A flower whose name is Greek for 'daughter of the wind'; also called the windflower.
ANGELICA: A tall herb whose candied stems decorate cakes; said to have been revealed by an angel as a cure.
ANISE: A herb (Pimpinella anisum) with liquorice-flavoured seeds, used in ouzo and pastis.
ANTHURIUM: A tropical plant with glossy, heart-shaped red flowers; its name means 'tail flower'.
APRICOT: A tree (Prunus armeniaca) with orange stone fruit, first grown in China and Central Asia.
ARALIA: A plant of the ivy family with large divided leaves, grown as a houseplant.
ARBUTUS: The strawberry tree, an evergreen with red fruits that look like strawberries.
ARROWROOT: A tropical plant whose starchy root thickens sauces; once used to treat arrow wounds.
ASPEN: A poplar whose leaves tremble in any breeze; Utah's Pando grove is one aspen with a single root system.
ASTER: A daisy-like autumn flower whose name is Greek for 'star'.
ASTILBE: A shade plant with feathery plumes of flowers; its name means 'without shine' in Greek.
AZALEA: A flowering shrub, a kind of rhododendron; its name is Greek for 'dry', as it grows in dry soil.
BALSAM: A plant with seed pods that burst open when touched; also a fragrant resin from trees.
BAMBOO: A giant woody grass; some kinds grow nearly a metre a day, the fastest of any plant.
BANANA: A giant tropical herb (genus Musa), not a tree; bananas are technically berries.
BANYAN: A fig tree (Ficus benghalensis) whose aerial roots become new trunks; India's national tree.
BAOBAB: An African tree with a massive water-storing trunk, nicknamed the upside-down tree.
BARBERRY: A spiny shrub with sour red berries used in Persian rice dishes.
BARK: The protective outer layer of a tree's trunk and branches; cork and cinnamon both come from bark.
BASIL: A fragrant herb (Ocimum basilicum) from India, the key to pesto; its name means 'royal' in Greek.
BEECH: A smooth grey-barked tree (Fagus sylvatica); early books were written on beech tablets, giving us 'book'.
BEGONIA: A colourful flowering plant named after Michel Bégon, a French governor of Haiti.
BELLFLOWER: A plant with bell-shaped blue or white flowers (genus Campanula, 'little bell').
BERGAMOT: A citrus fruit whose oil flavours Earl Grey tea; also a herb named for its similar scent.
BINDWEED: A twining weed with white trumpet flowers that wraps tightly around other plants.
BIRCH: A slender tree with white papery bark (genus Betula), among the first to grow after the Ice Age.
BLACKBERRY: The bramble (Rubus fruticosus), whose berries are a free autumn treat in hedgerows.
BLOODROOT: A woodland wildflower whose root bleeds red sap, used as a dye by Native Americans.
BLOOM: A flower, or the state of flowering.
BLOSSOM: The flowers of a fruit tree, such as apple or cherry.
BLUEBELL: A woodland flower with drooping blue bells; Britain has about half the world's bluebells.
BLUEBERRY: A shrub with small blue berries, native to North America.
BONSAI: The Japanese art of growing miniature trees in pots; also a tree grown this way.
BORAGE: A herb (Borago officinalis) with star-shaped blue flowers that taste of cucumber.
BOXWOOD: A slow-growing evergreen shrub used for hedges and topiary; its dense wood was used for engraving.
BRACKEN: A large fern that covers hillsides and turns rust-brown in autumn.
BRAMBLE: A thorny, sprawling shrub, especially the blackberry.
BRANCH: A woody limb growing from the trunk of a tree.
BRIAR: A thorny, prickly shrub such as the wild rose; briar-root pipes come from tree heath.
BROCCOLI: A vegetable of the cabbage family whose name is Italian for 'little sprouts'.
BUCKEYE: A North American horse chestnut whose shiny nut looks like a deer's eye; the emblem of Ohio.
BUCKTHORN: A thorny shrub whose bark and berries were used as a purgative.
BUCKWHEAT: A plant grown for its grain-like seeds, though it is not a wheat or even a grass.
BUTTERCUP: A shiny yellow wildflower (genus Ranunculus); held under the chin, it shows if you like butter.
CABBAGE: A leafy vegetable (Brassica oleracea) bred from wild cabbage, along with kale, broccoli and sprouts.
CACTUS: A spiny succulent of the Americas that stores water in its thick stem.
CALENDULA: The pot marigold, whose petals soothe skin; named from the Latin for the first day of the month.
CAMASS: A blue-flowered wild lily of North America whose bulbs were a staple food of Native peoples.
CAMELLIA: A flowering evergreen shrub from Asia; tea comes from one species, Camellia sinensis.
CAMPION: A wildflower (genus Silene) with pink or white flowers, common in hedgerows.
CANNA: A tropical plant with bold leaves and bright flowers; its hard seeds were once used as shotgun pellets.
CANOLA: A variety of rapeseed bred in Canada for its cooking oil; the name comes from 'Canada oil'.
CANOPY: The upper layer of a forest formed by the treetops.
CARAWAY: A herb (Carum carvi) whose seeds flavour rye bread; one of the oldest cultivated spices.
CARDAMOM: A spice from the seed pods of a plant of the ginger family, native to India.
CARNATION: A frilly flower (Dianthus caryophyllus) with a clove-like scent.
CARROT: A root vegetable (Daucus carota); carrots were mostly purple until orange ones were bred in the Netherlands.
CATTAIL: A tall marsh plant with brown, sausage-shaped flower heads; also called bulrush.
CATTLEYA: A showy orchid named after William Cattley, an English plant collector.
CAULIFLOWER: A vegetable with a white head of tightly packed flower buds; its name means 'cabbage flower'.
CEDAR: A tall, fragrant conifer (genus Cedrus); the cedar of Lebanon appears on that country's flag.
CELANDINE: A small yellow flower that blooms early in spring; its name is Greek for 'swallow'.
CELERY: A plant (Apium graveolens) with crunchy stalks, descended from wild marshland celery.
CELOSIA: A flower with feathery or crested heads; its name is Greek for 'burning', for its flame-like plumes.
CHERRY: A tree (genus Prunus) with small stone fruits; Japan celebrates its blossom as sakura.
CHESTNUT: A tree whose nuts are roasted; the sweet chestnut was spread across Europe by the Romans.
CHICKWEED: A low, creeping weed with tiny white star-shaped flowers, eaten by chickens.
CHICORY: A blue-flowered plant whose roasted root was used as a coffee substitute.
CHIVE: A slender, onion-flavoured herb (Allium schoenoprasum) with edible purple flowers.
CILANTRO: The American name for coriander leaves, from the Spanish.
CLEMATIS: A climbing plant with showy flowers; its name comes from the Greek for 'vine branch'.
CLIVIA: A South African lily with orange flowers, named after Lady Clive, Duchess of Northumberland.
CLOVER: A low plant (genus Trifolium) with three-part leaves; a four-leaf clover is said to bring luck.
COLLARD: A leafy green of the cabbage family, a staple of the cooking of the American South.
COLUMBINE: A flower with spurred petals; its name is Latin for 'dove', as it looks like five doves.
COMFREY: A herb once called knitbone, used as a poultice for broken bones.
CONEFLOWER: Echinacea, a daisy with a cone-shaped centre, used as a herbal remedy for colds.
COREOPSIS: Tickseed, a yellow daisy-like flower whose seeds look like ticks.
CORIANDER: A herb (Coriandrum sativum) used for both leaves and seeds; some people think it tastes of soap.
CORNFLOWER: A blue wildflower once common in cornfields; Estonia's national flower.
COSMOS: A daisy-like flower from Mexico; Spanish priests named it after the Greek for 'order' and 'harmony'.
COTTONWOOD: A poplar whose seeds float away on cotton-like fluff.
COWSLIP: A yellow spring wildflower of meadows, a relative of the primrose.
CRABAPPLE: A small, sour wild apple, used to make jelly.
CRANBERRY: A low shrub of North American bogs with tart red berries, harvested by flooding the bog.
CRESS: A small peppery salad plant, often grown on damp paper in school classrooms.
CROCUS: A small spring flower grown from a corm; saffron comes from the stigmas of one species.
CROTON: A tropical shrub with bold, multicoloured leaves, popular as a houseplant.
CUCUMBER: A long green fruit of the gourd family, about 95 per cent water; from India.
CURRANT: A shrub (genus Ribes) with small black, red or white berries.
CYCLAMEN: A plant with swept-back petals, grown from a tuber; its name comes from the Greek for 'circle'.
CYPRESS: A tall evergreen conifer, often planted in cemeteries as a symbol of mourning.
DAFFODIL: A yellow spring flower (genus Narcissus), the national flower of Wales.
DAHLIA: A Mexican flower named after the Swedish botanist Anders Dahl; it is Mexico's national flower.
DAISY: A small white flower with a yellow centre; its name comes from 'day's eye', as it opens at dawn.
DANDELION: A yellow weed whose name comes from the French 'dent de lion', lion's tooth, for its leaves.
DELPHINIUM: A tall plant with spikes of blue flowers; its name is Greek for 'dolphin', for the shape of its buds.
DIANTHUS: The genus of pinks and carnations; its name is Greek for 'flower of the gods'.
DILL: A feathery herb (Anethum graveolens); its name may come from the Norse 'dilla', to lull, for its soothing use.
DOGWOOD: A tree or shrub whose hard wood was once used to make skewers, called 'dags'.
DUCKWEED: The smallest flowering plants, tiny leaves floating on ponds; a favourite duck food.
EDELWEISS: A white woolly flower of the Alps; its name is German for 'noble white'.
ELDER: A shrub (Sambucus nigra) whose flowers make cordial and whose berries make wine.
ELDERBERRY: The dark purple berry of the elder, used for wine and syrups.
ENDIVE: A bitter leafy chicory used in salads.
ERICA: The genus of heaths, low evergreen shrubs with tiny bell-shaped flowers; most come from South Africa.
EUCALYPTUS: An Australian tree, food of the koala; its oil clears the nose.
EUPHORBIA: Spurge, a varied genus with milky, irritating sap; the poinsettia is one.
EVERGREEN: A plant that keeps its leaves all year round.
FENNEL: A feathery herb (Foeniculum vulgare) with an aniseed flavour; Marathon in Greece is named after it.
FENUGREEK: A herb whose seeds and leaves flavour curries; its name means 'Greek hay'.
FERN: A flowerless plant that spreads by spores rather than seeds; ferns are older than the dinosaurs.
FLAX: A blue-flowered plant (Linum usitatissimum) grown for linen fibre and linseed oil since ancient Egypt.
FORSYTHIA: A shrub covered in yellow flowers in early spring, named after the Scottish botanist William Forsyth.
FOXGLOVE: A tall plant with tube-shaped flowers; it is poisonous but gave the heart drug digitalis.
FREESIA: A fragrant flower from South Africa, named after the German doctor Friedrich Freese.
FUNGUS: A living thing such as a mushroom or mould, once grouped with plants but now its own kingdom.
GARDENIA: A fragrant white-flowered shrub, named after the Scottish naturalist Alexander Garden.
GARLIC: A pungent bulb (Allium sativum) eaten by the builders of Egypt's pyramids for strength.
GAZANIA: A South African daisy whose flowers close at night and in dull weather.
GENTIAN: A mountain plant with intense blue flowers; its bitter root flavours bitters and aperitifs.
GERANIUM: A flowering plant whose name is Greek for 'crane', for its beak-shaped seed pods.
GERBERA: A large, bright daisy from South Africa, named after the German botanist Traugott Gerber.
GINGER: A tropical plant (Zingiber officinale) whose spicy root is used in cooking and to ease nausea.
GINKGO: A tree (Ginkgo biloba) unchanged for 200 million years; a 'living fossil' from China.
GINSENG: A plant whose forked root is prized in Chinese medicine; its name means 'man root'.
GLADIOLUS: A tall flower with sword-shaped leaves; its name is Latin for 'little sword'.
GLOXINIA: A houseplant with velvety bell-shaped flowers, from Brazil.
GOLDENROD: A plant with plumes of yellow flowers that bloom in late summer.
GOOSEBERRY: A thorny shrub with tart green berries, a traditional sauce for goose and mackerel.
GORSE: A spiny yellow-flowered shrub of heaths; its flowers smell of coconut.
GOURD: A hard-shelled fruit of the squash family, dried and used as bowls, bottles and instruments.
GRAPEVINE: A climbing vine (Vitis vinifera) that bears grapes.
GRASS: A plant with narrow leaves and jointed stems; wheat, rice, maize and bamboo are all grasses.
GREENS: The leaves of plants such as cabbage, spinach or kale, eaten as vegetables.
HARDWOOD: Wood from broad-leaved trees such as oak and maple, as opposed to conifers.
HAWTHORN: A thorny shrub with white May blossom, often planted as a hedge.
HAZEL: A shrub (Corylus avellana) whose nuts are hazelnuts; forked hazel twigs were used for water divining.
HAZELNUT: The nut of the hazel; Turkey grows most of the world's hazelnuts.
HEATHER: A low evergreen shrub (Calluna vulgaris) with purple flowers that covers moors.
HELIOTROPE: A fragrant purple flower that smells of cherry pie; its name means 'turning to the sun'.
HELLEBORE: The Christmas rose, a winter-flowering plant that is highly poisonous.
HEMLOCK: A highly poisonous plant of the carrot family; Socrates was executed with it.
HERB: A plant whose leaves, seeds or flowers are used for flavour, scent or medicine.
HEUCHERA: Coral bells, a plant grown for its colourful leaves, named after the German botanist Johann von Heucher.
HIBISCUS: A tropical flower with large, showy petals; its dried flowers make a tart red tea.
HICKORY: A North American nut tree with tough wood used for tool handles and for smoking food.
HOLLY: An evergreen (Ilex aquifolium) with prickly leaves and red berries, a symbol of Christmas.
HOLLYHOCK: A tall cottage-garden flower, said to have been brought to Europe from the Holy Land by crusaders.
HONEYSUCKLE: A climbing plant with sweet-smelling tubular flowers whose nectar can be sucked from the base.
HOPS: The cone-like flowers of the hop vine (Humulus lupulus), used to give beer its bitterness.
HORSERADISH: A plant whose hot, pungent root is grated to make a sauce for roast beef.
HORSETAIL: A primitive, spore-bearing plant; its relatives grew as tall as trees before the dinosaurs.
HOSTA: A shade-loving plant grown for its large leaves, from China, Japan and Korea; slugs love it.
HOYA: The wax plant, a climbing vine with starry flowers, named after the English gardener Thomas Hoy.
HYACINTH: A fragrant spring bulb flower, named after Hyacinthus, a youth in Greek myth.
HYDRANGEA: A shrub whose flowers turn blue in acidic soil and pink in alkaline soil.
IMPATIENS: Busy Lizzie, whose seed pods burst at a touch; its name means 'impatient'.
IRIS: A sword-leaved flower named after the Greek goddess of the rainbow, for its many colours.
IXORA: A tropical shrub with clusters of red or orange flowers, named after a Hindu deity.
JASMINE: A climbing shrub with fragrant white or yellow flowers, used in perfume and tea.
JONQUIL: A kind of daffodil with several fragrant flowers on each stem; its name comes from Spanish for 'rush'.
JUNIPER: An evergreen conifer whose berry-like cones flavour gin.
KALANCHOE: A succulent from Madagascar with clusters of tiny flowers; some grow baby plants on their leaves.
KALE: A hardy leafy cabbage (Brassica oleracea) that survives frost; it tastes sweeter after a cold snap.
KELP: Giant brown seaweed of cool coasts; some kelp grows half a metre a day and forms underwater forests.
KOHLRABI: A vegetable with a swollen, turnip-like stem; its name is German for 'cabbage turnip'.
KUDZU: A fast-growing Japanese vine that can climb a foot a day; known as 'the vine that ate the South' in the US.
LANTANA: A tropical shrub with clusters of flowers that change colour as they age.
LARCH: A conifer (genus Larix) that, unusually, sheds its needles every autumn.
LARKSPUR: A tall plant with spurred flowers said to look like a lark's claw.
LAUREL: The bay tree (Laurus nobilis); ancient Greeks crowned victors with laurel wreaths.
LAVENDER: A fragrant purple-flowered herb from the Mediterranean, long used to scent washing and baths.
LEEK: A mild onion relative (Allium porrum) with a long white stem; a national emblem of Wales.
LEGUME: A plant of the pea family, such as beans or lentils, whose roots enrich the soil with nitrogen.
LENTIL: A legume (Lens culinaris) with lens-shaped seeds; the optical lens is named after it.
LICHEN: A partnership of a fungus and an alga, growing on rocks and trees; a sign of clean air.
LILAC: A shrub (Syringa vulgaris) with fragrant purple or white flower clusters, native to the Balkans.
LILY: A tall flower of the genus Lilium grown from a bulb; lilies are poisonous to cats.
LIME: A small green citrus fruit; British sailors ate limes against scurvy, earning the nickname 'limeys'.
LINDEN: The lime tree (genus Tilia), with fragrant flowers that make a calming tea.
LISIANTHUS: A rose-like flower from the prairies of North America, popular in bouquets.
LOBELIA: A plant with small blue flowers, named after the Flemish botanist Matthias de l'Obel.
LOTUS: A water plant (Nelumbo nucifera) sacred in Hinduism and Buddhism; its leaves repel water.
LUPINE: A plant with tall spikes of pea-like flowers; its name comes from the Latin for 'wolf'.
MAGNOLIA: A tree with large, fragrant flowers, one of the oldest flowering plants, older than bees.
MAHOGANY: A tropical tree of the Americas with prized reddish-brown timber.
MAIZE: A tall cereal grass (Zea mays), first grown in Mexico about 9,000 years ago; called corn in America.
MANDRAKE: A plant with a forked root that legend said would scream when pulled up.
MANGROVE: A tree that grows in salty tidal water on tropical coasts, on stilt-like roots.
MAPLE: A tree (genus Acer) with lobed leaves; its sap is boiled down to make maple syrup.
MARANTA: The prayer plant, whose leaves fold upward at night as if in prayer.
MARIGOLD: A bright orange or yellow flower, used in Mexico's Day of the Dead celebrations.
MARJORAM: A sweet herb (Origanum majorana) related to oregano.
MEADOWSWEET: A wildflower of damp meadows; it gave the chemical from which aspirin was first made.
MESQUITE: A thorny desert tree of the Americas whose wood gives smoky flavour to barbecues.
MILKWEED: A plant with milky sap, the only food of monarch butterfly caterpillars.
MIMOSA: A plant whose leaves fold up when touched (Mimosa pudica); also the yellow-flowered silver wattle.
MINT: A fragrant herb (genus Mentha) named after Minthe, a nymph in Greek myth turned into the plant.
MISTLETOE: A parasitic plant that grows on trees; kissing under it is a Christmas custom.
MONKSHOOD: A deadly poisonous plant with hood-shaped purple flowers; also called wolfsbane.
MOSS: A small, flowerless plant with no roots that grows in soft mats in damp, shady places.
MULBERRY: A tree whose leaves are the main food of silkworms; its berries look like blackberries.
MUSHROOM: The fruiting body of a fungus, often shaped like an umbrella.
MUSTARD: A plant of the cabbage family whose seeds are ground to make the condiment.
MYRTLE: A fragrant evergreen shrub of the Mediterranean, sacred to Venus in Roman myth.
NARCISSUS: The genus of daffodils, named after the youth in Greek myth who fell in love with his reflection.
NASTURTIUM: A trailing plant with peppery edible flowers; its name means 'nose twister'.
NEMESIA: A South African bedding plant with bright, two-lipped flowers.
NETTLE: A plant (Urtica dioica) with stinging hairs; young nettles make soup and were once woven into cloth.
NIGHTSHADE: A family of plants including deadly nightshade, but also potatoes, tomatoes and peppers.
OATS: A cereal grass (Avena sativa) grown for its grain; a staple of Scottish porridge.
OKRA: A green seed pod (Abelmoschus esculentus) from Africa, used to thicken gumbo; also called ladies' fingers.
OLEANDER: An evergreen Mediterranean shrub with showy flowers; every part of it is poisonous.
OLIVE: An evergreen Mediterranean tree (Olea europaea); some olive trees are over 2,000 years old.
ONION: A bulb vegetable (Allium cepa); cutting it releases a gas that makes eyes water.
ORCHID: A flower of the largest plant family, with about 28,000 species; vanilla comes from an orchid.
OREGANO: A herb (Origanum vulgare) whose name is Greek for 'joy of the mountains'.
OXALIS: Wood sorrel, a clover-like plant with sour-tasting leaves; its name is Greek for 'sour'.
PALM: A tree with a tall unbranched trunk and a crown of large leaves; coconuts and dates grow on palms.
PANSY: A garden flower with a face-like pattern; its name comes from the French 'pensée', a thought.
PAPAYA: A tropical fruit tree from Central America; its sap tenderises meat.
PAPYRUS: A tall reed of the Nile that ancient Egyptians made into paper; the word 'paper' comes from it.
PARSLEY: A leafy herb (Petroselinum crispum) whose name means 'rock celery' in Greek.
PARSNIP: A sweet, pale root vegetable, used as a sweetener in Europe before sugar was common.
PEACH: A downy stone fruit (Prunus persica) that first grew in China, despite its name meaning 'Persian'.
PEAR: A sweet fruit tree (Pyrus communis) related to the apple; pears ripen best off the tree.
PEAT: Partly rotted moss and plants built up in bogs over thousands of years, once burned as fuel.
PECAN: A hickory tree of the southern US; its name comes from an Algonquian word for a nut cracked with a stone.
PELARGONIUM: The garden geranium, from South Africa; its name is Greek for 'stork'.
PENTAS: A shrub with star-shaped five-petalled flowers loved by butterflies; its name is Greek for 'five'.
PEONY: A shrub with large, lush flowers, named after Paeon, physician to the Greek gods.
PEPEROMIA: A small houseplant with thick, often patterned leaves; its name means 'like a pepper'.
PEPPERCORN: The dried berry of a climbing vine from India, ground to make black pepper.
PEPPERMINT: A mint that is a natural cross of watermint and spearmint, rich in cooling menthol.
PERIWINKLE: A trailing evergreen with blue flowers (genus Vinca), often used as ground cover.
PETAL: One of the coloured, leaf-like parts of a flower that attract pollinating insects.
PETUNIA: A trumpet-shaped garden flower from South America, related to tobacco.
PHILODENDRON: A tropical climbing houseplant; its name is Greek for 'tree-loving'.
PHLOX: A plant with clusters of bright flowers; its name is Greek for 'flame'.
PINE: An evergreen conifer (genus Pinus) with needles in bundles; some bristlecone pines are over 4,000 years old.
PLANTAIN: A starchy cooking banana; also a common lawn weed with ribbed leaves.
PLUM: A stone fruit tree (Prunus domestica); dried plums are prunes.
PLUMERIA: Frangipani, a tropical tree with fragrant flowers used in Hawaiian leis.
POINSETTIA: A Mexican shrub with red leaves around tiny flowers, named after the US diplomat Joel Poinsett.
POPLAR: A fast-growing tree (genus Populus); the tall Lombardy poplar lines many European roads.
POPPY: A flower with papery red petals; the red poppy is a symbol of remembrance for war dead.
PORTULACA: Moss rose, a succulent with bright flowers that open in the sun.
POTATO: A starchy tuber (Solanum tuberosum) first farmed in the Andes of Peru about 8,000 years ago.
PRIMROSE: A pale yellow spring flower (Primula vulgaris); its name means 'first rose'.
PUMPKIN: A large orange squash; the biggest grown weighed over a tonne.
QUINCE: A tree whose hard, fragrant fruit is cooked into jelly; marmalade was first made from quince.
RADICCHIO: A bitter red-leaved chicory from Italy.
RADISH: A crunchy, peppery root vegetable (Raphanus sativus) that can be ready to eat in under a month.
RAGWEED: A weedy plant whose pollen is a major cause of hay fever.
RAMBLER: A climbing rose with long, flexible stems.
RANUNCULUS: The genus of buttercups; its name is Latin for 'little frog', as many grow near water.
RASPBERRY: A shrub with soft red berries (Rubus idaeus, after Mount Ida in Greece).
REDBUD: A small North American tree whose pink flowers bloom straight from the bare branches.
REDWOOD: The coast redwood (Sequoia sempervirens) of California, the tallest tree on Earth at over 115 metres.
REED: A tall grass of wetlands, used for thatching roofs and for the reeds of woodwind instruments.
RHODODENDRON: A flowering evergreen shrub whose name is Greek for 'rose tree'.
RHUBARB: A plant with tart red stalks eaten as a fruit; its leaves are poisonous.
RICE: A cereal grass (Oryza sativa) grown in flooded paddies; it feeds more than half the world.
ROSE: A thorny shrub (genus Rosa) with fragrant flowers; rose hips are rich in vitamin C.
ROSEMARY: A fragrant herb whose name means 'dew of the sea', as it grows on Mediterranean coasts.
RUTABAGA: The swede, a root vegetable that is a cross between a cabbage and a turnip; the name is Swedish.
SAFFRON: The world's costliest spice, from the hand-picked stigmas of a purple crocus.
SAGE: A grey-leaved herb (Salvia officinalis) whose name comes from the Latin 'salvere', to be healthy.
SAGEBRUSH: A silvery, aromatic shrub that covers the deserts of the American West.
SALVIA: A large genus of plants including sage, with spikes of bright flowers.
SASSAFRAS: A North American tree whose root once flavoured root beer.
SCABIOSA: The pincushion flower, once used to treat scabies, which gave it its name.
SCALLION: A spring onion, harvested young before the bulb forms.
SEAWEED: Large algae that grow in the sea, eaten in Japan and Wales and used to thicken ice cream.
SEDGE: A grass-like plant of wet ground; 'sedges have edges', with triangular stems.
SEDUM: A succulent, also called stonecrop, often grown on green roofs.
SEEDLING: A young plant grown from a seed.
SEQUOIA: The giant sequoia of California, the most massive tree on Earth; named after a Cherokee scholar.
SESAME: One of the oldest oilseed crops; its pods burst open when ripe, perhaps the origin of 'open sesame'.
SHAMROCK: A three-leaved clover, the emblem of Ireland, said to be used by St Patrick to explain the Trinity.
SHRUB: A woody plant smaller than a tree, with several stems from the base.
SNAPDRAGON: A flower that opens like a dragon's mouth when its sides are squeezed.
SNOWDROP: A small white flower that blooms in late winter, often pushing up through snow.
SORGHUM: A drought-hardy cereal grass from Africa, grown for grain, syrup and fodder.
SORREL: A leafy herb (Rumex acetosa) with a sharp lemony taste from oxalic acid.
SOYBEAN: A legume from East Asia whose beans give tofu, soy sauce and oil.
SPEARMINT: A mint (Mentha spicata) with pointed, spear-shaped leaves, used in chewing gum.
SPINACH: A leafy vegetable (Spinacia oleracea) from Persia, made famous by Popeye.
SPROUT: A new shoot of a plant; also short for Brussels sprout.
SPRUCE: An evergreen conifer (genus Picea) with short needles; the traditional Christmas tree.
SQUASH: A fruit of the gourd family, such as courgette or pumpkin; first grown in the Americas.
STOCK: A garden flower (Matthiola) with a strong clove-like scent, especially in the evening.
STRAWBERRY: A low plant with red fruits whose seeds sit on the outside; not botanically a berry.
STRELITZIA: The bird of paradise flower from South Africa, named after Queen Charlotte of Mecklenburg-Strelitz.
SUCCULENT: A plant with thick, fleshy leaves or stems that store water, such as a cactus.
SUGARCANE: A tall grass from New Guinea whose stems are crushed for sugar.
SUMAC: A shrub whose dried red berries are a tangy Middle Eastern spice.
SUNFLOWER: A tall plant (Helianthus annuus) whose young flower heads follow the sun across the sky.
SYCAMORE: A large maple whose winged seeds spin like helicopters as they fall.
TAGETES: The genus of marigolds, from the Americas; named after Tages, an Etruscan god.
TANSY: A yellow button-flowered herb once used to keep flies away and to flavour Easter cakes.
TARO: A tropical plant (Colocasia esculenta) grown for its starchy root; used to make Hawaiian poi.
TARRAGON: A herb with a liquorice-like flavour, essential to béarnaise sauce; its name means 'little dragon'.
THISTLE: A prickly plant with purple flower heads, the national emblem of Scotland.
THYME: A small aromatic herb (Thymus vulgaris); Roman soldiers bathed in thyme for courage.
TOADFLAX: A wildflower with yellow snapdragon-like flowers.
TOBACCO: A plant (Nicotiana tabacum) of the Americas whose leaves are dried for smoking; named after Jean Nicot.
TOMATO: A fruit (Solanum lycopersicum) from South America; Europeans once thought it poisonous.
TORENIA: The wishbone flower, whose stamens form a wishbone shape; from tropical Asia and Africa.
TRILLIUM: A woodland flower with parts in threes: three leaves, three petals.
TRUNK: The main woody stem of a tree.
TUBEROSE: A night-scented flower from Mexico, prized in perfume; it grows from a tuber, not a rose.
TULIP: A spring bulb flower from Central Asia; in 1630s Holland single bulbs sold for the price of a house.
TUMBLEWEED: A plant that breaks off when dry and rolls in the wind, scattering its seeds.
TURMERIC: A plant of the ginger family whose bright yellow root colours curry.
TURNIP: A root vegetable (Brassica rapa); the first Halloween lanterns were carved from turnips.
TWIG: A small, thin shoot or branch of a tree or shrub.
VANILLA: A climbing orchid from Mexico whose cured pods give vanilla flavour; its flowers are usually pollinated by hand.
VERBENA: A plant with clusters of small flowers; vervain, one species, was a sacred herb in ancient rituals.
VERONICA: Speedwell, a plant with blue flower spikes, named after St Veronica.
VETCH: A climbing plant of the pea family, grown to feed livestock and enrich the soil.
VINCA: The periwinkle, a trailing plant; one species gives drugs used to treat childhood leukaemia.
VINE: A plant with a long, trailing or climbing stem, such as the grapevine.
VIOLET: A small flower (genus Viola) with heart-shaped leaves; its scent briefly dulls the sense of smell.
WALNUT: A tree (genus Juglans) grown for its nuts and its dark, fine-grained timber.
WATERCRESS: A peppery leafy plant that grows in clear running water.
WATERLILY: A water plant with floating leaves; Monet painted the ones in his garden at Giverny.
WEED: Any plant growing where it isn't wanted; one gardener's weed is another's wildflower.
WHEAT: A cereal grass (genus Triticum) first farmed in the Fertile Crescent about 10,000 years ago.
WILLOW: A tree (genus Salix) of damp ground; its bark gave the chemical behind aspirin.
WISTERIA: A climbing vine with hanging clusters of purple flowers; some live for over a century.
WOLFSBANE: Monkshood, a poisonous plant once used to bait traps for wolves.
WORMWOOD: A bitter herb (Artemisia absinthium) used to make absinthe.
YARROW: A feathery herb (Achillea millefolium) named after Achilles, who used it to heal soldiers' wounds.
YUCCA: A spiky desert plant of the Americas, pollinated only by yucca moths.
ZINNIA: A bright daisy-like flower from Mexico, named after the German botanist Johann Zinn; it has flowered in space.
ZUCCHINI: The courgette, a small summer squash; the name is Italian for 'little squash'.
